issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s statutory interest in commercial premises remains heritable after termination of the contractual tenancy when the rent-control law does not restrict its inheritance, and the heirs may continue to receive the law’s protection against eviction.
material_facts: The tenant leased a shop for commercial use, and the landlord terminated the lease by notice.
The tenant remained in possession after termination, and the landlord accepted rent from her until her death, leaving her a statutory tenant under the rent-control law.
The heirs succeeded to her interest by intestate succession and remained in possession of the shop.
The heirs had not carried on the business with the tenant during her lifetime.
issues.conclusion: The tenancy interest was heritable despite termination of the contractual tenancy, and the heirs succeeded to it and were entitled to the rent-control law’s protection against eviction except in accordance with that law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 3(vii)(a) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, a person continuing in possession after termination of tenancy remains a tenant unless a decree for eviction has been passed. Section 13(1) protects a tenant from eviction except on grounds specified by the Act. Applying the ordinary law of succession, including the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the Court held that the statutory tenant’s interest in commercial premises is heritable where the Act contains no contrary restriction. The Court relied on Damadilal v. Parashram, which treated a statutory tenant as retaining an interest in the premises; Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar, which held that termination does not itself extinguish the tenant’s estate or make commercial tenancy non-heritable; V. Dhanpal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal; and the earlier cases J.C. Chaterjee v. Sri Kishan and Anand Niwas (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Anandji Kalyanji Pedhi. It distinguished Bhavarlal Labhchand v. Kanaiyalal Nathalal Intawala, which concerned a testamentary transfer to a stranger.

rule.if: commercial_tenancy_ejectment_case and statutory_tenant_at_death and heirs_succeeded_by_intestacy and heirs_remained_in_possession and no_lawful_inheritance_restriction

predicates.commercial_tenancy_ejectment_case: A landlord seeks eviction of the heirs of a tenant from premises leased for commercial or business use.
predicates.statutory_tenant_at_death: The original tenant remained in possession under rent-control protection when the tenant died.
predicates.heirs_succeeded_by_intestacy: The tenant’s heirs succeeded to the tenant’s interest through intestate succession.
predicates.heirs_remained_in_possession: The heirs continued in possession of the premises after the tenant’s death.
predicates.no_lawful_inheritance_restriction: No applicable law restricted inheritance of the tenant’s interest in the commercial premises.
predicates.heirs_inherit_tenancy_and_receive_protec: The heirs inherit the tenancy interest and may remain protected from eviction except in accordance with the applicable rent-control law.

issues.definition: When a commercial tenant protected by rent-control law dies while a statutory tenant, heirs who succeed by intestacy and remain in possession inherit the tenancy and its protection if no applicable law restricts that inheritance.

issues.legal_issue: A prospective amendment imposing conditions on heirs’ continuation of a commercial tenancy does not divest tenancy rights that vested in the heirs before the amendment took effect.
material_facts: The tenant died and succession to her tenancy interest opened before the amendment to the rent-control law came into force.
The heirs succeeded to the interest under the ordinary law of succession and remained in possession.
The amendment was prospective and conditioned the continuation of commercial tenancy on the heirs having carried on business with the tenant as family members until the tenant’s death.
The heirs had not carried on business with the tenant during her lifetime.
issues.conclusion: The prospective amendment did not apply to the heirs’ already vested tenancy rights, and its new qualification did not bar their continuation in possession.
issues.legal_principle: A vested right acquired under the law applicable when succession opens cannot be divested by a later prospective amendment. The Court applied the ordinary law of succession and the rule that a vested inheritance cannot be taken away except by a valid retrospective law. It considered Section 3(vii)(b), as introduced by the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Amendment Act, 1976, and held that its new conditions did not govern succession that had already opened. The Court relied on the principles concerning heritable statutory tenancy in Damadilal v. Parashram and the Constitution Bench decision in Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar.

rule.if: commercial_tenancy_ejectment_case and tenancy_inheritance_vested_before_amendment and amendment_is_prospective and heirs_lack_new_qualification

predicates.commercial_tenancy_ejectment_case: A landlord seeks eviction of heirs from premises leased for commercial or business use.
predicates.tenancy_inheritance_vested_before_amendm: The tenant died and the heirs acquired the tenancy interest before the relevant amendment took effect.
predicates.amendment_is_prospective: The amendment applies prospectively rather than retrospectively.
predicates.heirs_lack_new_qualification: The heirs do not meet a condition newly imposed by the amendment for continuing the tenancy.
predicates.later_amendment_does_not_divest_vested_t: The later amendment does not remove tenancy rights that had already vested in the heirs.

issues.definition: If commercial tenancy rights vested in heirs before a prospective amendment and the heirs lack its new qualification, the amendment does not divest those vested rights.
